The Sri Lankan Civil War was a war from 1983 to 2009 between the government of Sri Lanka and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), who fought for an independent Tamil state in the north and east of the island. It killed somewhere between 80,000 and over 100,000 people.

Its roots lay in the rift between the Sinhalese majority and the Tamil minority after independence in 1948. The Sinhala Only Act of 1956 made Sinhala the sole official language, and later university quotas and settlement schemes deepened Tamil anger. The Black July riots of 1983, in which Sinhalese mobs killed hundreds of Tamils, began the war.

  • The LTTE, led by Velupillai Prabhakaran, became a feared rebel army that used suicide bombers and child soldiers. It killed India's former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 and Sri Lanka's president Premadasa in 1993.
  • An Indian peacekeeping force fought the LTTE from 1987 to 1990 and withdrew.
  • A ceasefire brokered by Norway in 2002 slowly fell apart. The Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004 struck both sides, and quarrels over aid deepened the conflict.

The army crushed the LTTE in 2009, killing Prabhakaran. Tens of thousands of civilians are thought to have died in the final months, trapped between the two sides. The war left a large Tamil diaspora and shaped the region's politics. Even in wartime there were moments of unity, such as when Sri Lanka won the Cricket World Cup in 1996.
